1. Introduction

In modern software engineering, a personal developer portfolio is much more effective than a static paper resume. It provides a live, verifiable platform where recruiters, evaluators, and academic mentors can examine practical coding competency, UI/UX aesthetics, and architectural decisions. As a final-semester Computer Science and Engineering student at Daffodil International University, I designed and built this portfolio website from scratch to showcase my core web computing knowledge (Semantic HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and React component modularity) along with real university projects.

2. Part-A: Planning & Website Structure (2.0 Marks)

2.1 What the Website Is, Target Audience, and Design Justification

What it is: A responsive, dark-first personal portfolio website featuring single-page navigation, academic coursework matrices, interactive UI showcases, and a validated contact channel.

Target Audience: (1) Technical recruiters assessing front-end proficiency and clean code habits; (2) University course teachers evaluating syllabus compliance and semantic structuring; (3) Engineering classmates collaborating on software projects.

Why this design was chosen: I selected a modern dark-first design (deep navy-blue background #0a0f1d with electric blue #0284c7 and cyan accents) because dark themes reduce eye strain during extended code reviews and create high visual contrast. I utilized fluid typography using CSS clamp() and flexbox/grid containers to ensure flawless readability across desktop monitors, tablets, and mobile smartphones without horizontal overflow.

The website follows a unified Single Page Application (SPA) architecture with persistent navigation links that scroll smoothly to distinct content sections, coupled with an interactive Case Study modal sub-view:

3. Part-B: Implementation (2.0 Marks)

3.1 Standard HTML Document Structure & Tag Adherence

The project strictly follows the W3C HTML5 standard. The entry point index.html defines the standard declaration <!DOCTYPE html>, language attribute <html lang="en">, responsive viewport metadata <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">, character encoding <meta charset="UTF-8">, search-engine optimization tags, and linked Google web fonts (Plus Jakarta Sans, Inter, JetBrains Mono) within the <head> before the <body> container.

3.2 Semantic Tags, Lists, Images, and Hyperlinks

  • Headings & Paragraphs: Structured hierarchical tags (<h1> for page title, <h2> for major sections, <h3> for project and skill titles, and <p> for explanatory text) establish an accessible document outline.
  • Ordered & Unordered Lists: Unordered lists (<ul>, <li>) present academic highlights, bullet points, and core competencies. Ordered lists (<ol>, <li>) present procedural steps in the live presentation demo plan.
  • Images: Responsive images (<img>) include the author's profile portrait (profile-picture.jpeg) with descriptive alt text, plus SVG vector iconography.
  • Hyperlinks: Internal anchor links (href="#skills", href="#contact") provide rapid page jumps, while external links (href="https://github.com/Sultana-Asma" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer") safely connect to external repositories.

3.4 Explanation of Three Key Code Snippets

Snippet 1: Sticky Navigation Bar with Active Scroll-Spy (Navbar.jsx)

useEffect(() => {
  const handleScroll = () => {
    setScrolled(window.scrollY > 16);
    const sectionIds = navigation.map((item) => item.href.replace("#", ""));
    let current = "";
    for (const id of sectionIds) {
      const el = document.getElementById(id);
      if (el) {
        const rect = el.getBoundingClientRect();
        if (rect.top <= 140 && rect.bottom >= 140) {
          current = `#${id}`;
          break;
        }
      }
    }
    setActiveSection(current);
  };
  window.addEventListener("scroll", handleScroll, { passive: true });
  return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", handleScroll);
}, [navigation]);

What the code does: Automatically calculates the viewport position of each section during scrolling and highlights the active menu item.
Why used: It provides visual feedback so visitors always know where they are on the page without manual reloads.

Snippet 2: Interactive Rain Simulation on HTML5 Canvas (VillageSimulationCanvas.jsx)

const drawRain = (ctx) => {
  ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(180, 210, 255, 0.65)";
  ctx.lineWidth = 1.2;
  raindrops.forEach((drop) => {
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(drop.x, drop.y);
    ctx.lineTo(drop.x + drop.wind, drop.y + drop.length);
    ctx.stroke();
    drop.y += drop.speed;
    if (drop.y > riverTop) {
      createRipple(drop.x, drop.y); // Trigger ripple wave
      drop.y = -10;
      drop.x = Math.random() * canvas.width;
    }
  });
};

What the code does: Animates falling rain vectors on a 2D HTML5 Canvas and generates expanding circular water ripples on river collision.
Why used: Solves the problem of demonstrating native C++ OpenGL desktop graphics coursework directly inside the web browser.

Snippet 3: Anti-Spam Honeypot & Form Validation (ContactSection.jsx)

// 1. Silent Honeypot Trap
if (formData.website && formData.website.trim() !== "") {
  setStatus("success");
  setStatusMessage("Message processed.");
  return; // Trap automated bots without alerting them
}
// 2. Regex Email & Consent Validation
const emailRegex = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;
if (!formData.email.trim() || !emailRegex.test(formData.email.trim())) {
  newErrors.email = "Please enter a valid email address.";
}
if (!formData.consent) {
  newErrors.consent = "Please check the box to confirm consent.";
}

What the code does: Checks email syntax using regular expressions, requires legal user consent, and catches spam bots using an invisible input field.
Why used: Protects student inboxes from automated spam while maintaining an accessible, friendly user interface.

4. Part-C: Form, Testing & Justification (1.0 Marks)

4.1 Contact Form Implementation with All Required Control Types

The Contact section features a robust, fully controlled HTML form satisfying all rubric specifications:

  • Text Input: <input type="text" name="name" required> captures the sender's full name.
  • Email Input: <input type="email" name="email" required> captures email address with browser validation.
  • Dropdown Select: <select name="subject"> allows choosing inquiry categories (Internship, Project, General).
  • Radio Buttons: <input type="radio" name="contactMethod"> lets users choose between Email and Phone/WhatsApp.
  • Checkbox: <input type="checkbox" name="consent" required> provides formal communication consent.
  • Textarea: <textarea name="message" rows="4" required> collects multiline inquiry details.
  • Submit Button: <button type="submit"> with loading spinner and accessibility states.

0242310005101682 • Sultana Asma Islam Part-C: Justification, Conclusion & References

4.3 Real Engineering Problems Faced & Solutions

Problem 1: Showcasing Desktop C++ OpenGL Graphics on the Web:
The Challenge: Our university computer graphics project was compiled as a native desktop binary (.exe), making it impossible to run directly in web browsers.
Solution: Instead of forcing evaluators to download an executable, I engineered an in-browser interactive modal simulation using an HTML5 <canvas> 2D context. I mathematically recreated the Day, Night, and Rain lighting and ripple physics directly in JavaScript.

Problem 2: Image Distortion & Squashing on Multi-Column Cards:
The Challenge: Initially, screenshots with differing aspect ratios stretched and appeared vertically squashed when placed inside flexible multi-column cards.
Solution: I enforced modern CSS rules: aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; object-position: top;. This locked all preview windows to standard widescreen dimensions, ensuring zero distortion across all screen sizes.

4.4 Justification of Design & Technology Choices

  • Why Semantic HTML5 instead of generic <div> tags: Elements like <header>, <nav>, <section>, and <footer> provide clear semantic hierarchy, enhance screen-reader accessibility (WCAG), and make code significantly easier to maintain.
  • Why Single-Page Architecture with Section Identifiers: Navigating through internal anchors avoids disruptive page refreshes, preserves JavaScript state (e.g., simulation modes), and feels significantly faster to recruiters.
  • Why Centralized CSS Variables: Defining global variables (--bg-surface, --accent-blue) allows instantaneous global theme changes and guarantees visual consistency across all components.

4.5 Future Roadmap & Planned Improvements

  1. Node.js & Express REST API: Build a dedicated backend to receive contact form submissions and trigger instant email notifications.
  2. Database Integration (MongoDB / PostgreSQL): Store visitor messages, inquiries, and project feedback securely in a persistent database.
  3. Production Deployment with Custom Domain: Host the live website on a global CDN (e.g., Vercel / GitHub Pages) with an SSL/TLS HTTPS certificate and a custom domain.

5. Conclusion

Building this portfolio website was an invaluable hands-on learning experience. It bridged classroom theory with real front-end engineering practices—including semantic HTML5 document structures, responsive CSS layouts, accessible forms, and JavaScript event management. More importantly, it taught me how to analyze user needs, solve technical constraints (like porting OpenGL concepts to HTML5 Canvas), and document my engineering decisions in a structured analytical manner.
